claims.text: Enacted as Public Law 118-31, Division A, Title XVIII, Subtitle C ('Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena'), secs. 1841-1843, 137 Stat. 699-707. Sec. 1841 carries the note '44 USC 2107 note'. Approved 22 December 2023.

claims.source: Comparison of BILLS-118s2226es Div. G with PLAW-118publ31 Subtitle C
claims.text: Subtitle C corresponds one-to-one to secs. 9004, 9005 and 9006 of the Senate-passed Division G. Senate secs. 9001-9003 and 9007-9015 - including the Review Board (9007-9009), eminent domain over recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence (9010), disclosure of other materials and additional study (9011), termination (9013) and authorization of appropriations (9014) - have no enacted counterpart.

Sec. 1841(a)(1)(C) puts the phrases 'technologies of unknown origin' and 'non-human intelligence' into enacted federal law as categories of record the Archivist must collect, '(or equivalent subjects by any other name with the specific and sole exclusion of temporarily non-attributed objects)'.

Sec. 1842(g)(2)(D) requires full public disclosure of each UAP record within 25 years of its first creation unless the President personally certifies identifiable harm outweighing the public interest.
Sec. 1843(a) vests the postponement determination in 'the original classification authority' rather than in any independent reviewer.

Sec. 1843(b) permits Senior Agency Officials to withdraw records from the Collection, with 60 days' notice to Congress, on their own determination that the records are unrelated and properly classified.
Sec. 1842(a)(2) prohibits destruction, alteration or mutilation of any UAP record and bars reclassification of anything already publicly disclosed before enactment.

claims.source: Inference from comparison of Sec. 9009(c)(1) with Sec. 1843(a)
claims.text: Retaining the 'clear and convincing evidence' standard while transferring its application from an independent board to the original classifier preserves the appearance of the Senate's regime while removing its effect.

desc: What Congress actually enacted is a records-transfer statute with the enforcement removed. Sec. 1841 orders the Archivist to establish the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection, requires physical integrity and original provenance to be preserved, requires public availability within 30 days of transmission and online within 180 days thereafter, and assigns continuing oversight to six committees. Sec. 1842 bars destruction, alteration or mutilation of any UAP record, bars withholding or reclassification of anything already public, bars withholding of records created outside the Federal Government, and gives agency heads 300 days to review and organise. Sec. 1843 is where it fails. Postponement may be ordered where 'the original classification authority makes a determination that there is clear and convincing evidence' of harm — the clear and convincing standard survives, but the person applying it is the classifier rather than an independent board, which converts a check into a self-certification. Senior Agency Officials may unilaterally withdraw records from the Collection on a determination that they are both unrelated to UAP and properly classified, needing only to notify Congress 60 days beforehand. Where disclosure is postponed the agency head must notify congressional leadership within 15 days with a reason. There is no appeal, no de novo review, no subpoena and no mechanism reaching material rather than paper.
